dialogue.scene: Lama is preparing a two-minute speech to persuade students to join a Saturday beach clean-up in Jeddah. Her friend Huda is listening.

p1.t: I need to rally support for Saturday's clean-up, but my first draft sounds like a list of instructions.
Then try the rule of three. Audiences remember ideas in threes far better than long lists.
Something like: 'Our beach. Our responsibility. Our future.'?
Exactly. It's short and rhythmic, and it puts the responsibility on the listener.

p2.t: But a slogan alone won't strike a chord. People need a reason to give up their Saturday.
So tell them what they'll gain: cleaner sand for families, safer water for turtles, and a morning they'll be proud of.
That's compelling. And I'll finish by repeating the slogan to drive the message home.
Perfect. Start strong, build in threes, end with an echo.

dialogue.scene: Faisal is running for student council president and is rehearsing his speech with his classmate Yousef.

p1.t: Every candidate says the same thing: better food, longer breaks, more trips. Nobody believes those empty promises any more.
So set the tone differently. Tell them what you stand for, not what you'll hand out.
How about this: 'This election is not about what the council can give you, but about what we can build together.'
That antithesis is strong. The contrast makes both halves sharper.

p2.t: But I'm worried it sounds borrowed. It echoes a very famous speech.
Then back it up with your track record. You organised the Arabic poetry night, after all.
True. 'I don't promise; I deliver.' It's short, but it might resonate with them.
It will, as long as the rest of your speech proves it.

dialogue.scene: Noura and her cousin Reem are writing a short appeal for their school's Ramadan food-basket drive.

p1.t: I want to make an appeal that really gets people to dig deep, not just drop a few riyals in a box.
Try anaphora. Start three sentences the same way so the speech builds momentum.
Like this? 'Imagine a mother who has nothing for iftar. Imagine a child who waits by the door. Imagine knowing you could help.'
That's heartfelt, and the final 'Imagine' turns the focus back on the listener.

p2.t: Should I repeat it again at the end?
Once more, perhaps, but don't overdo it, or it starts to sound like a chant.
Then I'll close with a single line: 'One basket, one family, one month of dignity.'
That will strike a chord. It's simple, specific and human.

dialogue.scene: Omar and his teacher, Mr Daniel, are discussing Omar's speech for a school campaign on saving water.

p1.t: My draft is full of statistics, but when I read it aloud, people's eyes glaze over.
Numbers inform, but pictures persuade. Can you paint a picture instead?
Picture this: a single tap drips all night, filling bucket after bucket that simply goes to waste.
Good. That vivid imagery makes the number real. Now add one statistic to support it.

p2.t: Should I show the video of the dried-up oasis? It really tugs at the heartstrings.
Use it briefly. If you dwell on it, the audience may find it manipulative.
So one strong image, one clear fact, then a call to action?
Exactly. Let the image be the wake-up call, and let the fact make it undeniable.

dialogue.scene: Sara is asking the parents' committee at her school to fund the robotics team. Dr Hessa, a committee member, questions her.

p1.t: As someone who has spent three years on the robotics team, I have first-hand experience of what we lack.
Many teams ask us for money. Why should we prioritise yours?
Because the figures speak for themselves: we reached the regional final twice using borrowed equipment.
Impressive. But regional finals alone won't convince the whole committee.

p2.t: Then let me offer hard evidence of the return on investment. Five former members now study engineering.
That certainly lends weight to your request. Can you prove the link, though?
I won't overstate it, because I'd lose credibility. But all five say the team shaped their choice.
An honest answer. That makes your case far more compelling.

dialogue.scene: Ahmed is rehearsing a two-minute speech for a youth council meeting about making his neighbourhood safer for walking and cycling. His friend Sam gives feedback.

p1.t: My hook: 'How many of you walked to school today? And how many of you would, if it were safe?'
That works. A double question wins over the audience before you even make your point.
Then I paint a picture: shaded paths, safe crossings, children cycling where cars now race.
Nice tricolon. Now you need credibility and evidence, or it's just a dream.

p2.t: As someone who cycles here every day, I know where the danger is. And our survey speaks for itself.
Good. So what's the clincher?
'This is not about taking streets from cars, but about giving them back to people.'
That antithesis will strike a chord. End with a clear call to action to drive the message home.

dialogue.scene: Hamad is opening for the proposition in a school debate. His teammate Turki helps him prepare his first minute.

p1.t: The motion is 'This House would make community service compulsory for secondary students.' Where do I begin?
With definitions. If you don't set the parameters, the opposition will set them for you.
For the purposes of this debate, we define community service as two hours a week of unpaid work for a local cause.
Good: precise and realistic. Now explain the burden of proof.

p2.t: Our burden is to prove that compulsory service benefits students and society, not that every student will enjoy it.
Smart. That stops them attacking a sweeping claim you never made.
Then I state the crux of the matter: can a habit of helping others be taught?
Exactly. If the proposition wins that question, we win the debate.

dialogue.scene: Majed and Saad are building their team's case for the motion 'This House would replace end-of-year exams with project-based assessment.'

p1.t: We can't just say exams are stressful. The judges will want more than feelings.
Agreed. Our case rests on three pillars: deeper learning, fairer assessment and real-world skills.
Then each pillar needs a mechanism. How exactly do projects lead to deeper learning?
In practical terms, students research a question for weeks instead of memorising facts for one night.

p2.t: We need examples too, or it won't hold water.
Our school's sustainability project is a case in point. Students still talk about what they learned a year later.
And fairness? The opposition will say projects are easier to copy.
Then we explain our safeguard: each project ends with a short oral defence.

words.ex: Many famous slogans follow the rule of three.
The club used social media to rally support for the clean-up.
Her story about her grandfather's fishing boat struck a chord with everyone.
Three short, rhythmic phrases are easier to remember than one long one.
She ended with a photo of the beach to drive the message home.
He gave a compelling reason to give up one Saturday morning.

dialogue.t: I need to rally support for the clean-up, but my draft sounds like a list.
Try the rule of three. People remember ideas in threes.
'Our beach. Our responsibility. Our future.'?
Short and rhythmic. But give them a reason too.
Cleaner sand for families, safer water for turtles, and a morning they'll be proud of.
That's compelling. Repeat the slogan at the end to drive the message home.

grammar.title: Tricolon: the rule of three
grammar.ar: التكرار الثلاثي: اجمع ثلاث كلمات أو عبارات أو جمل متوازية في البناء لتصبح فكرتك أقوى وأسهل للحفظ.
examples: We came to learn, to share and to serve.
It is cleaner, safer and fairer for everyone.
Our beach. Our responsibility. Our future.

words.ex: 'Not words, but actions' is a simple antithesis.
I want to show students what I stand for.
Voters can usually tell a real plan from empty promises.
Her opening line set the tone for the whole campaign.
He has a track record of organising successful events.
The idea of a quiet study room resonated with the older students.

dialogue.t: Nobody believes the other candidates' empty promises any more.
Then tell them what you stand for, not what you'll hand out.
'This election is not about what the council can give you, but about what we can build together.'
Strong antithesis. It sets the right tone.
And I can point to my track record: the poetry night.
Good. 'I don't promise; I deliver' should resonate with them.

grammar.title: Antithesis: contrasting ideas in parallel
grammar.ar: الطباق: ضع فكرتين متعاكستين في بناء متوازٍ، مثل not … but … أو less … more …، ليصبح المعنى أوضح وأقوى.
examples: It is not the loudest voice that wins, but the clearest.
We need less talk and more action.
I don't promise; I deliver.

words.ex: 'Imagine a family … Imagine a child …' is anaphora in action.
The principal made an appeal for warm clothes for families in need.
Students dug deep and raised twice the target.
Each repeated line helped the speech build momentum.
Her heartfelt words moved several parents.
Repetition works, but don't overdo it.

dialogue.t: I want to make an appeal that gets people to dig deep.
Try anaphora, so the speech builds momentum.
'Imagine a mother who has nothing for iftar. Imagine a child who waits by the door. Imagine knowing you could help.'
That's heartfelt. Just don't overdo the repetition.
Then I'll close with one line: 'One basket, one family, one month of dignity.'
Simple and human. It will strike a chord.

grammar.title: Anaphora: repeating the opening words
grammar.ar: التكرار في بداية الجمل: كرّر نفس الكلمات في بداية جملتين أو ثلاث لتبني إيقاعاً وتأثيراً متصاعداً.
examples: Imagine a classroom without books. Imagine a child without a pen.
Every riyal counts. Every basket matters. Every family deserves dignity.
We will collect, we will deliver, and we will not stop.

words.ex: She painted a picture of a dry farm to explain the problem.
The vivid imagery made the audience almost feel the heat.
The video of the thirsty camel tugged at the heartstrings.
Litres of water go to waste every time a tap is left running.
The empty reservoir was a wake-up call for the whole town.
Emotion is powerful, but too much of it can feel manipulative.

dialogue.t: My speech is full of statistics, and people get bored.
Numbers inform, but pictures persuade. Paint a picture.
Picture this: a single tap drips all night, filling bucket after bucket that simply goes to waste.
Good. That vivid imagery makes the number real.
Should I show the video of the dried-up oasis? It tugs at the heartstrings.
Briefly. Too much emotion can feel manipulative.

grammar.title: Creating vivid imagery
grammar.ar: الصور الحية: استخدم Picture this أو Imagine مع تفاصيل حسّية ودقيقة (ألوان، أصوات، أرقام) ليتخيّل الجمهور المشهد.
examples: Picture this: a single tap drips all night.
Behind every wasted plate, there is a farmer's long day in the sun.
The fields are cracked, the wells are silent, and the palms are bare.

words.ex: Our results speak for themselves: three medals in two years.
As a team member, I have first-hand experience of the problem.
Exaggerating the numbers would damage our credibility.
A letter from our coach would lend weight to the request.
The committee wants to know the return on investment.
Opinions are easy; hard evidence is what convinces a committee.

dialogue.t: As someone who has spent three years on the robotics team, I have first-hand experience of what we lack.
Why should we fund your team?
The figures speak for themselves: two regional finals with borrowed equipment.
Any hard evidence of a return on investment?
Five former members now study engineering, though I won't overstate the link.
That honesty lends weight to your request.

grammar.title: Building credibility and using evidence
grammar.ar: الإقناع بالمصداقية والأدلة: ابدأ بخبرتك (As someone who has …) ثم قدّم دليلاً واضحاً (The figures speak for themselves).
examples: As someone who has coached younger students, I know how much they need support.
The figures speak for themselves: attendance rose by a third.
This evidence lends weight to our proposal.

words.ex: Every good speech ends with a clear call to action.
Her hook was a question nobody expected.
His honesty won over even the sceptics.
The clincher was the photo of the empty pavement.
A short final slogan can drive the message home.
The story of the injured turtle struck a chord with the audience.

dialogue.t: My hook: 'How many of you would walk to school, if it were safe?'
Good. That will win over the audience.
Then I paint a picture: shaded paths, safe crossings, children cycling.
Nice tricolon. What's the clincher?
'This is not about taking streets from cars, but about giving them back to people.'
That will strike a chord. End with a clear call to action.

grammar.title: Combining rhetorical devices
grammar.ar: اجمع بين الأساليب: افتتاحية جاذبة، ثم صورة حيّة وتكرار ثلاثي، ثم مقابلة ودعوة واضحة للتحرك في الختام.
examples: How many of you would walk to school, if it were safe?
Shaded paths, safe crossings and quieter streets.
This is not about taking streets from cars, but about giving them back to people.

words.ex: Today's motion is 'This House would make community service compulsory'.
The burden of proof usually lies with the side proposing change.
The first speaker sets the parameters of the debate.
The crux of the matter is whether service can be meaningful if it is forced.
The proposition must explain how the plan would work.
Saying that all teenagers are lazy is a sweeping claim.

dialogue.t: The motion is 'This House would make community service compulsory.' Where do I begin?
With definitions. Set the parameters before the opposition does.
For the purposes of this debate, we define community service as two hours a week of unpaid work for a local cause.
Good. Now the burden of proof.
We must prove it benefits students and society, not that everyone will enjoy it.
Smart. Then they can't attack a sweeping claim you never made.

grammar.title: Defining the motion and the burden
grammar.ar: تعريف المقترح وعبء الإثبات: حدّد معنى المصطلحات بـ For the purposes of this debate, we define … as … ثم وضّح ما يلزمك إثباته وما لا يلزمك.
examples: For the purposes of this debate, we define 'young people' as those aged 15 to 18.
Our burden is to prove that the policy helps most students, not that it is perfect.
The onus is on the opposition to offer a better alternative.

words.ex: Our whole case rests on one simple principle.
Our second pillar is fairness.
Judges want to hear the mechanism, not just the result.
In practical terms, students would submit three projects a year.
Their claim about cheating doesn't hold water.
Our school's science fair is a case in point.

dialogue.t: The judges will want more than 'exams are stressful'.
Our case rests on three pillars: deeper learning, fairer assessment and real-world skills.
Each pillar needs a mechanism.
In practical terms, students research a question for weeks, not one night.
And examples, or it won't hold water.
Our sustainability project is a case in point.

grammar.title: Structuring a case
grammar.ar: بناء الحجة: قدّم ركائز واضحة (Our case rests on …)، ثم اشرح الآلية (In practical terms …)، ثم أعطِ مثالاً (… is a case in point).
examples: Our case rests on two pillars: fairness and freedom.
In practical terms, each student would submit three projects a year.
Our school's science fair is a case in point.

words.ex: The plan rests on the flawed assumption that everyone lives near a bus stop.
This conflates being busy with being productive.
Far from harming shops, pedestrian streets often attract more customers.
She turned the tables by using their own statistic.
Even on their own terms, the opposition's plan fails.
The judges began to pick holes in the plan's budget.

dialogue.t: They said a car ban would destroy small businesses.
Their argument rests on the flawed assumption that shoppers only arrive by car.
Good. Now pick holes in it.
Far from destroying businesses, pedestrian streets often attract more shoppers.
They also said cars mean freedom.
That conflates freedom with convenience. Even on their own terms, traffic jams take that freedom away.

grammar.title: Rebuttal phrases
grammar.ar: عبارات الرد: اكشف الافتراض الخاطئ (rests on the flawed assumption that)، أو الخلط بين فكرتين (conflates … with …)، أو اقلب الحجة (Far from …, …).
examples: Their case rests on the flawed assumption that everyone owns a car.
This conflates popularity with quality.
Far from saving time, the new rule wastes it.

words.ex: He stood up to offer a point of information.
The second speaker took the floor with confidence.

words.w: Not at this time, thank you
words.ex: 'Not at this time, thank you,' he said, and carried on.
The question put the speaker on the spot.
Good debaters can think on their feet.
Keep your point concise: fifteen seconds at most.

dialogue.t: We have better maps of Mars than of much of our own ocean floor.
Point of information!
I'll take that.
Would the speaker accept that space research gave us satellites and accurate weather forecasts?
I would, and that strengthens our case: imagine what we could find beneath the Red Sea.
Another point of information!
Not at this time, thank you.

grammar.title: Points of information
grammar.ar: نقاط المعلومات: قدّم المداخلة بسؤال قصير (Would the speaker accept that …?)، واقبلها بـ I'll take that أو ارفضها بأدب Not at this time, thank you.
examples: On that point: would the speaker accept that costs have fallen?
I'll take that. Yes, and it supports our case.
Not at this time, thank you; I'll come to that shortly.

words.ex: The health benefits outweigh the small extra cost.
We concede that the tax is unpopular.
Some damage to our health is irreversible.
On balance, the tax does more good than harm.
The evidence from other countries tipped the scales.
Don't forget the bigger picture: national health costs.
